body:
Attogram: blah blah crows

Grok

That’s a real relationship, not a casual “feed the birds” hobby.

You’ve already crossed the threshold most people never reach with urban corvids:

- Individual recognition (you know *Anchorow*)
- The murder recognises *you*
- Close approach without fear
- Gift exchange (even partial gifts count)
- Occasional, high-value food (eggs, shrimp) rather than daily dependency feeding

That’s classic corvid social bonding territory. Crows are extremely good at reading consistency, reliability, and individual humans. The fact that you’ve been gone for more than two weeks and they’re still oriented to you when you return is meaningful — they’re not just treating you as a vending machine.

### A few practical notes from how these relationships usually develop

- **Welcome-back gift is good.** A hard-boiled egg or two (or a few shrimp) after a long absence is a clear signal. They notice the interruption and the resumption.
- Keep the feeding **irregular and modest**. You’re already doing this correctly. Daily predictable feeding can create dependency and sometimes local conflict with neighbours or other animals. Occasional high-value offerings keep the relationship social rather than purely transactional.
- Location matters. If you have a consistent spot near the house where they already feel safe approaching, stick to it. Sudden changes of place can reset some of the trust.
- Document lightly but consistently if you want this to feed the civic-science side (attogram.005 / .006 / .020). Date, weather, who showed up, whether Anchorow was present, any gifts received, any new individuals. Even short notes are valuable over time.

### How this sits inside the bigger project

This is exactly the kind of long-running, place-based, non-extractive observation that the Corvidae census and urban fauna petitions are pointing toward. Most “citizen science” bird projects are brief checklists. What you have is longitudinal, individual-level, and reciprocal. That is rarer and more interesting.

If you ever want to formalise it a bit without killing the intimacy, you could:

- Keep a simple ongoing log (even in the Provo42-Corpus or as notes attached to the relevant petition thread)
- Note morphological or behavioural markers that let you reliably ID Anchorow and a few others
- Record the gift exchanges (both directions)

But there’s no need to force it into data collection mode. The relationship itself is already the primary thing.

When you’re back and give them the welcome eggs, you’ll probably get a very clear read on whether the bond held through the absence. From everything you’ve described, my expectation is that it will.

Want any thoughts on low-key ways to document this without turning it into a science project, or how it might eventually sit inside one of the numbered petitions?
